https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/08/bale.text: Menü Kereső Vaddisznó szaladt le a Kossuth téri metróba Belföld frissítve Thüringer Barbara Sarkadi Zsolt Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Az M2-es metró helyett baleset miatt a Deák Ferenc tér és a Déli pályaudvar között pótlóbusz közlekedik, amely a Batthyány tér állomást nem érinti” – adta hírül szombaton délelőtt 11 óra után pár perccel a BKK Info a Facebook-oldalán. Nem sokkal később kiderült, hogy egy vaddisznó szabadult be valahogy a Kossuth térre, majd lement az álló mozgólépcsőn a metróaluljáróba. Erről még videó is készült, a Szeretlek Magyarország oldalon jelent meg, íme: A BKK 13 óra után kiadott közleménye szerint amikor a Kossuth Lajos téri állomás forgalmi ügyeletese észlelte, hogy az egyik, üzemen kívüli mozgólépcsőn egy vaddisznó sétál lefelé a peronszintre, értesítette az állomásra éppen akkor beérkező metró vezetőjét, aki arra kérte a peronon tartózkodó utasokat, hogy biztonságuk érdekében szálljanak vissza a metrókocsikba. „A rendkívüli helyzetben az állat rövid időre bejutott az egyik vonatba, de senki nem sérült meg. A vaddisznó ezt követően elhagyta a szerelvényt, majd egy, a pályára vezető szolgálati lépcsőn lejutott a sínek közé, és a várakozó metró alá húzódott” – írták. Hozzátették, az állomást azonnal kiürítették, ezért nem is sérült meg senki. Ezután érkeztek meg az állat befogására a katasztrófavédelem munkatársai. Miután kiderült, hogy a vaddisznó sérült, a helyszínre riasztott hatósági állatorvos megvizsgálta és felmérte az állapotát, majd a lehetséges megoldásokat mérlegelve a kilövés mellett döntött. Azt egyelőre nem tudni, hogy a vaddisznó hol szerezte a sérüléseit, illetve, miért tévedt be az állomásra. Korábban megjelentek hírek arról is, hogy a kb. 60 kilós állatot elütötte a metró, és hogy ezután lőtte ki a rendőrség, de ezek nem voltak pontosak. „Egy vaddisznó miatt kellett pótlóbuszokat beállítani az M2 metró vonalán. Magam sem hittem volna, hogy egyszer ilyet kell leírnom... Hogy miként került a vaddisznó a Kossuth téri metróállomásra, azt most még senki nem tudja” – írta a Facebookon Karácsony Gergely főpolgármester. A metrópótlásra 30 autóbuszt csoportosított át a BKK, de azt írták, nem sokkal dél után már újraindult a közlekedés. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Telex shop További élő árfolyamok! Mutasd! Friss hírek

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar By Soutik Biswas India correspondent Published 2 hours ago Well past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother. Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety. "Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says. An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts. The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves. By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it. Image caption, Baruah quit journalism to concentrate on animal husbandry The scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam. The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps. The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated. For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound. "This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says. Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime. Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km. Image caption, A 97-year-old Lokada Duarah was carried onto a banana tree trunk and taken to safety after floodwaters rose around her home Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, A boy uses a makeshift banana raft to navigate floodwaters in Assam She had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building. Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'. Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it. She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed. None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says. The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly. Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages. About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp. Image caption, Baruah and her family abandoned their home nearly a day after the water began rising For five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil. Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats. Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill. But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before? Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley, a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms". The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A family shelters inside a tent in Sivasagar district, among more than 5,000 people lodged in 252 relief camps Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Amit Giri holds a photo of his father, Siv Sankar Giri, who died in the floods, outside their damaged home in Sivasagar. He is among 100 people killed in the floods. As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251. In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat. Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology. Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam. "What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography. For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal. Image caption, Only 60 of Baruah's goats survived the floods She has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week. Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have. So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life. She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance. Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods â and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee? "No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before." "We will have to learn to coexist with the floods." https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/thi.text: The Budapest Times Thirty-six wasted years: PM blames predecessors as drought exposes climate failures The previous political elite deliberately neglected climate protection and climate change, the Prime Minister said on Monday in a pre-agenda address to the National Assembly. Péter Magyar announced that in August of this year, 28 percent more water is being retained in Hungary than a year ago. The Prime Minister said that a ministerial address opening with the words climate change, water scarcity, and climate change might seem unique and novel. He stated that after sixteen, or rather thirty-six, wasted years, it is not possible to make up for every failure in just three months, but the current drought situation also proves that addressing this set of problems is not an unnecessary luxury, “not a Western ideological deviation,” but rather one of the most important adaptations to changed circumstances — one that the previous political elite deliberately neglected. Based on the experiences of recent weeks, it appears that over the past decades, not only in parliament but throughout the entire government, confronting the drastically changed environmental conditions and preparing the steps necessary to avert climate catastrophe — in other words, genuine action — was effectively forbidden. He criticised the Orbán government for dissolving the Water Management Scientific Research Institute in 2012, and for Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s statement in 2023 that Hungary has a surplus of water and no water shortage. He also took issue with the fact that former Speaker of the House László Kövér said in 2019 that so many people were concerned about climate change only because of the brainwashing effect of the media, while in December 2025 former minister János Lázár acknowledged that water scarcity represents a brutal reality. “The philosophy of Fidesz governance was that this issue did not need to be addressed,” he said, adding that Fidesz and KDNP had misled even their own voters. Péter Magyar continued by saying that the regime change of 12 April had come at the last possible moment — indeed past the last moment — with regard to water management and climate protection as well. He indicated that they considered it important for environmental protection to have its own independent ministry, led by László Gajdos. He recalled that ahead of the new government’s first session, they had addressed the issues of drought and water retention at Ópusztaszer, having begun work “from the very first minute” — and not without results. This August, 28 percent more water is being retained in Hungary than a year ago. While 523 million cubic metres of water were stored at this time last year, this year 669 million cubic metres are being held in the landscape — he noted, describing this as a small step. Péter Magyar also spoke about the fact that, still this year, the environmental authority operating under the strictest conditions in Europe will begin its work. He recalled that, due to daily average temperatures, a third-level heat alert had to be issued again after June, and that the dry summer had driven the water level of the Danube to an unprecedented low that was already threatening the operation of the Paks nuclear power plant. When it became necessary, a defence working group was immediately formed, which — “in contrast to the earlier sham or operetta-style task forces” — drew on the expertise needed from every relevant field, he said. He assessed that it had become clear from the very start of the crisis that “the previous decades’ token measures, government by decree, and operetta-style politicking in various states of emergency” had produced no real results, and that the crisis threatening the country’s energy and water networks had caught the state administration almost entirely unprepared. He elaborated that in crisis management, the first and most important task had been to preserve nuclear safety, and there was no cause for concern in that regard going forward. The second task, he pointed out, was to avoid a so-called blackout — a potential collapse of the energy grid. He stressed that the continuous and safe operation of the grid had been ensured and would remain so in the period ahead. The Prime Minister elaborated that thanks to the immediate adoption of the necessary legislation and clear, honest communication that treated people and companies as partners, Hungary had pulled together, and during the critical period consumption had fallen by nearly 10 percent compared to projections, making it possible to preserve the stability of the energy system. He touched on the fact that the Paks plant had not had to be completely shut down so far — one turbine was still generating power — and that the reconnection of the third turbine in the second unit was currently under way, meaning that by evening two turbines were expected to be producing electricity. However, based on meteorological forecasts, virtually no rainfall was expected over the next ten days, so following a temporary rise, a further drop in water levels was to be anticipated, he said. Péter Magyar said that the plant’s employees were continuously working on solutions that would allow at least partial operation to be maintained. Péter Magyar said that exactly how much final damage the extraordinary circumstances of recent weeks and the unprecedented drought will cause to the economy — and within that, to the agricultural sector — may only be accurately estimated in the coming weeks, but it is already clear that frost and drought damage in the agricultural sector alone amounts to several hundred billion forints. The prime minister stressed that the entire state administration needs to be rebuilt, as Hungary is not prepared for crises of this kind. He reported that the Paks nuclear power plant had no safety plan for such low water levels, despite the fact that a water level of -98 centimetres had already been recorded in 2018. The first turbine had to be shut down at a water level of -107 centimetres, he said, adding that there was also no plan setting out who would be responsible for what in the event of a nationwide power outage. The prime minister accused the previous government of having taken no steps in recent years to prevent the economic and energy-related consequences of similar crises. Solar power plants were built without the necessary storage capacity, the construction of wind turbines was banned, while 1,000 billion forints of public money was spent on Paks II. The latter should already be operational, but currently only two large concrete basins have been completed, and during the planning process no consideration was given to what water levels would be required for cooling if the two plants were operated simultaneously, Péter Magyar noted. According to the prime minister, water management and energy policy have been marked by decades of backwardness and inaction on the part of governments in recent years. He argued that, lacking sufficient political courage, debates on these topics were never dared to be held, and that the issue of artificial water retention has been a taboo subject above all since Bős-Nagymaros. He stressed that, just as with the question of secret service files, the taboos surrounding water retention and nuclear energy also need to be put to rest, and that an open, honest conversation is necessary. For this reason, he called for these issues to receive adequate emphasis in the constitutional process and public dialogue beginning this autumn, and for the right to water, energy, and a sustainable environment to be precisely defined. Péter Magyar emphasized that the government is counting on every Hungarian both in the defence efforts that may be needed in the coming days and in finding good long-term solutions together. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/horror-wa.text: James Knuckey Sun, September 6, 2026 at 6:00 PM UTC 0 Vladimir Putin this week said it is a 'military secret' whether Russia will strike UK military sites (Image: Getty) Britain is "ripe" for Russian sabotage and must take action now to prepare for the threat, experts have warned. Labour is being urged to boost defences around critical infrastructure following a surge in incidents on mainland Europe . Many have been linked to Russia , with NATO and EU chiefs warning Moscow is becoming increasingly reckless. Illya Sekirin, a former adviser on drone warfare to the Ukraine government, said the West "underestimates" the threat with Russia now ramping up hybrid attacks. The former frontline drone pilot said Britain risks emboldening Vladimir Putin by failing to protect key sites. Police investigator at Leipzig/Halle after last month's attempted drone attack blamed on Russia (Image: Getty) He said the UK - and the rest of Europe - are particularly vulnerable to drones which have already been used to cause chaos in suspected Russian-linked incidents. "If you have the systems in place, Russia may think twice about trying to carry out some sort of hybrid drone attack with plausible deniability," Mr Sekirin told the Express. "Because it will know that most of the drones will not get through. It's really important for deterrence. Tensions are rising after Germany blamed Russia for the incident at Leipzig/Halle airport (Image: Getty) "But if things come to worse, you would like to have your critical infrastructure protected the best you can." It comes after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. The accusation, denied by Moscow, has triggered an intensifying diplomatic row as tensions between Russia and the West skyrocket . European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said such incidents have become the "new normal" and Europe must be ready to respond. Western officials have long alleged Russia is running a campaign of sabotage and disruption aimed at undermining support for Ukraine. The past month has seen a series of suspected Russian attacks targeting facilities linked to military support for Kyiv. NATO and the EU have vowed to step up pressure on Russia (Image: Getty) Incidents have taken place in Bulgaria , Italy , Estonia and Slovakia . While Poland has said Russia was likely behind a "deliberate arson" at a drone factory in the country last Monday. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out" for a fire at another facility in Lublin. Former Army intelligence officer Philip Ingram warned hybrid activity is rising and Britain is vulnerable. He said: "The UK is ripe for it. Putin will see us as weak and therefore will increase the number of attacks that he's got, in ways that he can try and put further pressure on the Government. "We need to brace ourselves for that." He said MI5 and counterterrorism police are "hugely under-resourced" for wider threats and urged national resilience plans to be accelerated as a priority. Defence sources say there is growing pressure on ministers to introduce the plans amid fears Russia could strike a critical sector in the coming years. Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Getty) An information campaign on the topic is being brought forward to the autumn , it is understood. Shane Mason, managing director at defence advisory firm Strategical, said the failed drone attack in Germany highlights the issue. He said: "Britain does not lack counter-drone technology or the expertise to keep developing the required solutions. We have some extremely capable people and companies in this area. "The bigger question is whether those capabilities are organised into a sufficiently coherent national system." Renewed Kremlin threats have only raised concerns Russia could wage an attack on British soil. Mr Putin this week said it is a "military secret" whether Russia will strike British military sites. Tensions are escalating between the two nations after the UK agreed to give Ukraine blueprints for Storm Shadow missiles . Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova warned the UK is "playing with fire" over the move. She also threatened to hit British military targets inside and outside Ukraine after UK-made missiles were used to strike Russian territory. Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has warned the UK is 'playing with fire' (Image: Getty) Shadow Defence Secretary James Cartlidge said the tensions show the need for defence spending to be boosted . He said: "With Russia ramping up its threats every day, Labour needs to be growing the armed forces and strengthening our deterrence. Instead, we have a Chancellor unable to commit to the very target of 3% Defence spending that he previously resigned over. "You can't protect Britain with words and vibes alone, tough choices are needed to properly fund our defence and national resilience. "Instead of being continuity Starmer on national security, Burnham should follow Kemi's lead by taking the tough decisions to cut welfare and fund defence, so that we can hit 3% by 2030 - sending a powerful signal to our adversaries that we will do whatever it takes to deter them." A spate of mysterious drone sightings across Europe in autumn last year prompted alarm among allies. Drones buzzed around critical infrastructure and military bases, while sightings near airports caused major travel disruption. British authorities are in touch with their German counterparts about the Leipzig/Halle Airport incident and are expected to remain in close contact as investigations continue, it is understood. The EU and NATO are working on a "drone wall" to protect European airspace from incursions. It is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027. A Government spokesperson said: "Keeping people safe and protecting national security is the first responsibility of government, which is why we are taking more steps than ever to ensure the resilience of our critical national infrastructure. "Defence has seen the biggest increase in defence spending since the Cold War, investing in air defences, drones and new technologies that will keep Britain safe, and increasing intelligence funding to meet rising demand to illuminate and deter threats. "We remain vigilant against potential threats, and Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this Government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies." Bhubaneswar: Nandankanan Zoological Park (NZP) authorities on Saturday released 36 animals and birds belonging to 11 new species into enclosures for public viewing as part of the state-level Wildlife Week celebrations. According to zoo sources, NZP received 58 animals and birds belonging to 14 species September 12 as a donation from the Radha Krishna Temple Elephant Welfare Trust in Gujarat. “The donated animals and birds are four zebras, four kangaroos, six Bennett’s wallabies, four ring-tailed lemurs, four tufted capuchins, four scarlet macaws, four blue-and-gold macaws, four green-winged macaws, four sulphur-crested cockatoos, four crowned cranes, four scarlet ibises, six meerkats, two casso waries and four blue wildebeests,” they said. “Of these, 36 animals and birds belonging to 11 species were released into enclosures for public viewing Saturday,” they said, adding that the animals and birds included zebras, kangaroos, Bennett’s wallabies, tufted capuchins, meerkats, scarlet ibises, sulphur-crested cock atoos, scarlet macaws, blue-and-gold macaws, green-winged macaws and crowned cranes. NZP Deputy Director Pradeep Mirase said the remaining ones belonging to three species would be released into enclosures in the coming days. The move will give visitors an opportunity to see the new animals and birds while strengthening the zoo’s objectives of wildlife conservation, education and awareness, the sources said. NZP authorities have also sought permission from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade to import two female red kangaroos from the Czech Republic and two zebras from another country. The authorities have received approval for the proposed imports, officials said.
